asks.title: What should happen with people still camping downtown?
asks.why: The District closed the camp behind Under One Roof for good on October 9, 2026, after a fire in September. Some people moved near Vancouver Street and Loggers Lane. The Province’s temporary housing has no site yet.
labels: Let people stay with more support

asks.title: Put the modular shelter somewhere other than the park near Junction Park
asks.why: Residents petitioned in April 2026 for a different site than Xwu’nekw Park on Loggers Lane. Council took the park off the list in June 2026.

asks.title: What should happen with the supportive housing planned at 39900 Government Road?
asks.why: BC Housing plans six storeys with 65 studio homes and support staff around the clock, run by Squamish Helping Hands. Construction is set to start in summer 2027.

asks.title: How should Squamish help open more licensed child care spaces?
asks.why: In May 2020 council endorsed a child care action plan with a goal of 720 new licensed spaces by 2029. The Province licenses and funds most child care; the District can offer land or space and speed up permits, as it did for the 36 space centre in Valleycliffe that opened in 2025.
labels: Build or lease District space for daycares
Only speed up permits for private daycares

asks.title: How should Squamish get more homes that people can rent?
asks.why: Rents are high and long term rentals are hard to find. Council decides rezonings for rental buildings, can put District land toward nonprofit housing, and since 2023 can waive development fees for nonprofit affordable rental homes.
labels: Put more District land toward nonprofit rentals
Put tax money toward buying rental buildings
Slow down until roads and services catch up

asks.title: Install the defibrillator at the Brennan Park pickleball and tennis courts this year
asks.why: Pickleball Squamish offered up to $4,000 toward it. A June 2026 staff report scheduled it for 2027.

asks.title: When should Squamish build more pickleball courts?
asks.why: In March 2026 staff asked council to hold off on new courts until the 2027 Parks and Recreation Master Plan looks at racket sports.

asks.title: Fix up the Eaglewind courts and reopen them for tennis
asks.why: The courts have sat unused since pickleball moved to Brennan Park. Staff recommended fixing them up for tennis, but in April 2026 council chose to explore other interim uses instead, not including pickleball.

asks.title: What should Brennan Park add next?
asks.why: A second rink and a second pool are both in the District’s long term vision, with no money set aside yet. A task force report is due in 2027.
labels: Both, even if taxes go up

asks.title: Fence the off leash dog area at John Hunter Park
asks.why: John Hunter Park is one of the off leash pilot sites. The District says it still needs a fence, with no timeline set.

asks.title: Build covered outdoor basketball courts
asks.why: Residents asked for covered outdoor courts in the 2021 feedback on the Brennan Park plan, so they can be used in the rain.

asks.title: Keep the new crosswalk and wider multi use lane on Highlands Way North
asks.why: Done in August 2026 after concerns about speeding in the school zone: a wider multi use lane with a buffer, no centre line, and a new crosswalk south of Pentland Way.

asks.title: Put raised crosswalks and new signs on Upper Mamquam Road
asks.why: Speeding and truck traffic. It is the District’s top ranked traffic calming site, and two raised crosswalks east of Aristotle Drive are set to be built in late October 2026.

asks.title: Put a raised crosswalk and new signs on Skyline Drive
asks.why: It is on the District's 2026 traffic calming list.

asks.title: Make the Highway 99 and Cleveland Avenue intersection safer
asks.why: The District says it has the most crashes of any intersection in town. The Province runs the highway, so council's role is to press for changes.

asks.title: Should downtown parking stay free?
asks.why: A 2023 study suggested paid parking downtown. Council chose to test it at Darrell Bay only.
labels: Paid only in the busiest spots

asks.title: Should Squamish help pay for a bus to Vancouver and Whistler?
asks.why: Squamish has local buses but no public bus to Vancouver or Whistler. It has been studied since 2015 and has stalled over who runs and pays for it.
labels: Yes, even with a small tax increase

asks.title: How much should property taxes go up in 2027?
asks.why: Property taxes rose 12.8% in 2026. The draft 2027 budget starts at a 10.4% increase, and the new council decides it, with adoption expected early 2027 (last year: January 13).

asks.title: How should Squamish speed up dike upgrades?
asks.why: Much of Squamish sits on a floodplain. The District raises dikes a section at a time, mostly when grants come through.

asks.title: Should Canada set up a permanent volcano observatory for the Sea to Sky?
asks.why: Federal scientists want to start Canada's first dedicated volcano watch on the peaks around Squamish, and the regional district has backed the idea. The Squamish-Lillooet Regional District board endorsed the proposal on October 30. The five-year project would cover Mount Garibaldi, Mount Cayley and Mount Meager from April 2027, if federal funding comes through.

asks.title: What should matter most in Squamish's 2027 budget?
asks.why: Squamish residents can tell the District where they would spend more and where they would spend less in 2027. The new council is now discussing the 2027 budget. The District asks people to follow along over the next few months and share input on LetsTalkSquamish.

asks.title: How should Brackendale get postal service now that its post office has closed?
asks.why: Brackendale's post office closed for good on October 31, 2026, 120 years after it opened. Canada Post could not fill the job or find a local business to host an outlet, so the service moves to Garibaldi Highlands. The neighbourhood itself is named after its first postmaster.
labels: Find a local shop to host an outlet
The District should help find a partner

asks.title: How should the Province handle Woodfibre's longer start up flaring?
asks.why: When Woodfibre LNG was approved in 2015, start up flaring was expected to last three to four weeks. The company now says commissioning will take six to eight months, with flaring several days a week. Comments on its air emissions permit are open until November 29.

asks.title: What should happen with Woodfibre's plan to release treated stormwater into Howe Sound?
asks.why: Woodfibre LNG says it has applied for a permit to send treated stormwater and drainage water from its plant into Howe Sound. People who may be affected can send written comments within 30 days of the last date the notice is posted. The application went to the BC Energy Regulator.
labels: Keep the water out of Howe Sound

asks.title: What should Squamish's new council work on first?
asks.why: Mayor Sean Easton and six councillors took their oaths Tuesday night in a packed room. In his first speech, Easton named four things he says Squamish needs fixed and told residents to measure council on results, not plans. A former mayor also told the new council that staff work for them.

asks.title: What should Squamish's 10 year jobs plan focus on most?
asks.why: The District of Squamish is creating a Labour Force Development Plan to help the community prepare for future jobs and workforce needs. Qatalyst Research Group and Synergy Foundation are supporting the work. It runs from April 2026 to March 2027, and the plan will guide actions over the next decade.
labels: Housing so workers can live here

asks.title: What matters most in Squamish's first urban forest strategy?
asks.why: The District of Squamish is developing its first Urban Forest Management Strategy. It will guide tree protection, planting and care on public and private land over the next 25 years. A community survey, an online mapping tool and an open house are planned, with details coming soon.
labels: Protect the big trees we have

asks.title: What should council aim for on 2027 District taxes?
asks.why: Every 1% is about $546,000 of services, or about $33 on an average home.

asks.title: If council lowers the increase, where should it look first?
asks.why: Each one has a trade off. Woodfibre LNG's money gets its own question below.
labels: Pause the repair savings step up
Shift more tax to business and industry

asks.title: Should Woodfibre LNG's tax money help pay for everyday costs?
asks.why: Today the District keeps the $7.24 million it gets from the plant for one time projects only.
labels: Yes, use it to keep taxes down
No, keep it for one time projects

asks.title: Squamish is behind on saving for repairs. How fast should it catch up?
asks.why: The main capital reserve starts 2027 at $3.9 million, below a $13.1 million target, and won't reach it until 2034 on the current plan.
labels: Faster, even if taxes rise more
Slower, to keep taxes down now

asks.title: Should the $580,000 community safety package go in the 2027 budget?
asks.why: Two bylaw officers, a Community Safety Plan and BC Housing support work, about $35 on an average home.

asks.title: What should council put first for 2027 to 2030?
asks.why: Pick the one that matters most to you. You can add your own.

asks.title: How should council show whether its plan is working?
asks.why: Last time progress was reported as the share of planned projects finished, not results like homes built or trips taken.
labels: Percent of projects done, as now

asks.title: The 2030 climate target is far off track. What should the new plan do?
asks.why: The goal was 45% below 2010. The District's own 2025 modelling says about 7% below if every action is done, mainly because the town is growing.
labels: Lower it to match the modelling
Drop it, focus on floods and fire

asks.title: Should residents get a say before council adopts its plan?
asks.why: Last time the draft was shown in public a week before the vote, with no survey first. B.C. law requires public consultation on the budget, not on a strategic plan, so it's council's choice.
labels: Yes, a survey and open sessions first
Yes, a chance to comment on a draft
No, council was elected to decide
